patent: Texas Instruments patent filed in 1990, the last continuation of a family going back to 1984. Inventor Larry Hornbeck is credited with inventing TI's Digital Micromirror Device (DMD) in 1987. Each pixel is a small aluminum mirror on thin torsion hinges over addressing electrodes. The patent adds landing electrodes held at the mirror's potential, so the mirror tip can touch down without welding. A bias voltage then makes the mirror bistable: it rests tilted one way or the other, set by a small address voltage. That two-state digital mirror became the basis of TI's DLP projection, which reached the market in the mid-1990s. Production DMDs later moved the hinges under the mirror and put a CMOS SRAM cell under each pixel.

figs.4: Defines the analysis variables. Top view: a square beam of side L hinged at corners 135 and 137, with the integration strip dx at distance x from the axis. Cross section: beam 130 and electrode 146 grounded, voltage phi_a on 142; tip 131 drops by z_T across gap z_0 as the beam rotates by theta. The right-hand brace groups the two views.
figs.5: Torque against normalized tip deflection alpha (alpha = 1: tip touches the electrode). The solid curves are electrostatic torque at three address voltages; the dashed straight line is the hinge restoring torque. For V1 the curves cross at P (stable) and Q (unstable). For V2 they touch at R, the last stable point. The V3 curve is above the line everywhere, so the beam collapses.
figs.6: Shown turned upright from the sideways drawing sheet. Summary of FIG. 5. The stable deflection alpha rises with address voltage phi_a until it reaches alpha_c = 0.54 at V_c. The dashed vertical arrow at V_c is the jump to alpha = 1.00 (collapse).
figs.7: Electrical schematic of pixel 20. The beam and both landing electrodes are tied to the differential bias V_B. The address signal phi_a drives electrode 46 (+) directly and electrode 42 (-) through the inverter triangle. The dashed lines show the beam tilted to -alpha and +alpha.
figs.8: Attractive torque for pixel 20 with the same voltage on both address electrodes. Torque toward 46 (tau_+, upper solid curve) and torque toward 42 (tau_-, lower solid curve) add up to the dashed net curve. The net curve passes through zero at alpha = 0. It stays finite at alpha = +/-1, because there the tip rests on a landing electrode.
figs.9: Variables for pixel 20: L' is how far address electrodes 42 and 46 extend under the beam, measured from the axis, against the half-diagonal L/sqrt(2). The landing electrodes and the beam sit at V_B; the address electrodes are driven to phi_- and phi_+.
figs.10: In FIGS. 10-13 the solid line is the restoring torque -tau_r and the dashed curve is the attractive torque at a given bias, both against deflection alpha. Here the bias is small: the dashed curve is smaller in magnitude than the line on both sides, so every deflection is pulled back to alpha = 0.
figs.11: At a higher bias the dashed curve crosses the line at P and -P near the ends. Past those points the beam snaps onto a landing electrode, so alpha = 0, +1 and -1 are all stable.
figs.12: At V_0 the dashed curve is tangent to the restoring line at the origin. alpha = 0 is no longer stable, and the beam falls to one landing electrode or the other.
figs.13: Above V_0 the dashed curve is steeper than the line through the origin. Any small tilt grows until the beam lands, so only alpha = +/-1 remain stable.
figs.14: Potential energy U against deflection for increasing bias V_B. At V_B = 0 there is a single valley at alpha = 0. At the intermediate biases, valleys at the landing points (dashed verticals at +/-1) form beside it, separated by humps. At V_B = V_0 the centre has become a hump and only the two landing valleys remain.
figs.15: Same layout as FIG. 7, biased for addressing: the beam and landing electrodes are at -|V_B|, electrode 42 is grounded, and electrode 46 is at phi_+ = +gamma|V_B|. This small address voltage chooses which way the beam falls when the bias is applied.
figs.16: Attractive torque with the small address voltage applied. The dashed curve is shifted so that it crosses zero at -|alpha_m| instead of the origin. An undeflected beam therefore feels a net torque toward +1 (landing electrode 41).
figs.17: Bistable switching. phi_+ and phi_- are complementary address levels (0 V or +gamma|V_B|). The bias phi_B sits at -|V_B| and returns briefly to 0 V; each time the bias comes back, the beam takes the side its address selects. The bottom trace alpha alternates between its two levels. Its lowest level is printed '+1'; the description calls it -1.
figs.18: Normalized torques (units tau_0, beta = 1/2). The upper curve is the single-electrode torque tau_+, the lower curve the differential torque tau_a = tau_0 Delta g. The dashed line marked SLOPE is the tangent of the lower curve at alpha = 0, from which the minimum bias V_0 is found. The steeper dashed line from the origin touches the upper curve at alpha_c (about 0.9) and height g_c.
figs.19: Net torque with no address voltage (gamma = 0, through the origin, no preferred direction) and with gamma = 0.1 (shifted up). The shifted curve meets the dashed restoring line at P, at -|alpha_p|. A beam starting to the right of that point goes to +1.
figs.20: Soft landing in the simplified pixel 120 with a narrowed electrode. The restoring line runs to tau_rL at alpha_L = 1. The attractive curve touches it at alpha_c, tau_c (collapse) and ends at tau_aL. The gap Delta tau_L between them at alpha = 1 is the torque left over when the tip lands.
figs.21: The same construction for pixel 20 biased at V_0. Curve (1), gamma = 0, and curve (2), gamma = 0.1, are labelled with their printed formulas. The landing torque Delta tau_L is read at alpha = alpha_L = 1.
figs.22: Holding torque. The upper curve (bias V_0) lands with excess torque tau_L. At the lower bias V_H the attractive curve meets the restoring line exactly at alpha = 1, so the landing torque is zero (tau_H = tau_rL). Below V_H the beam lifts off and returns to the analog point P.
figs.23: Deflection against bias, traced in the order (0)-(1)-(2)-(3)-(4) shown by the arrows. The beam rises along the analog curve to alpha_c at V_0, jumps to 1.0, and stays there as the bias is lowered. At V_H it drops back to the analog curve.
figs.24: Flatness margin. The solid curve is the attractive torque. The three dashed lines are the restoring torque for a flat beam (1), one with built-in tilt -|alpha_m| (2), and one tilted further (3). Line (2) crosses the axis where the curve does, so the beam has no preferred direction; with (3) it falls the wrong way. Delta alpha is the shift between (1) and (2).
figs.25: Plan view of address electrodes shifted by epsilon along the beam diagonal. The square is beam 30. The two diagonal-edged outlines are address electrodes 42 and 46. Each is drawn twice, solid and dashed, offset along the diagonal by the shift epsilon. The heavily hatched slivers +/-Delta A_1 and +/-Delta A_2 are the overlap gained and lost.
figs.26: Attractive torque for misalignment epsilon = 0 (1), epsilon_m (2) and larger (3), against the dashed restoring line. The short vertical arrow near alpha = 0.15 shows how far the torque drops as misalignment grows.
figs.27: FIG. 7 with balance electrodes added. 243 and 245 sit between the address and landing electrodes, and each is fed from a potentiometer between -|V_B| and ground; the potentiometers are the resistor symbols with arrows. Address signal phi drives 246 directly and 242 through the inverter.
figs.28: Torque lines for addressing the + electrode (left pair, tau_a+) and the - electrode (right pair, tau_a-). Solid lines are aligned (epsilon = 0); dashed lines have half the misalignment margin. The downward arrows show the shift. The axis intercepts give the angular margins: 1/2 alpha_m and alpha_m.
figs.29: First reset method. Each short spike phi_R (+V_R) on electrode 42 comes while the bias phi_B is at 0. phi_A is the address sequence: deflect, not deflect (dashed pulse), deflect. In the alpha trace the small dips below 0 are the brief kicks from the reset spikes; the dashed fall shows a beam that did not stick returning on its own.
figs.30A: Second reset method. A short spike to +V_R (or -V_R) on the bias line phi_B precedes each change of state. phi_A(+) and phi_A(-) select the side. alpha goes to +1, then to -1, then back to +1; the small steps are the reset bending and release.
figs.30B: Section along the hinge axis during the reset pulse. Beam 30 is pulled straight down toward substrate 22, bending hinges 34 and 36 instead of twisting them. The hinges spring it back up when the pulse ends.

glossary.def: A device that changes light pixel by pixel, for example a projector imager. Here each pixel steers reflected light by tilting a mirror.
TI's name for an array of electrostatically deflected micromirrors. In later products the D stands for 'digital'.
A thin, narrow metal strip that twists to let the mirror rotate and springs it back. Its stiffness sets the restoring torque.
A beam fixed at one end that bends down instead of twisting. It deflects in one direction only.
The voltage at which electrostatic attraction overpowers the hinge and the beam snaps all the way down. Usually called pull-in or snap-down today.
Tip deflection divided by the tip-to-electrode gap: 0 means flat, +/-1 means the tip is touching down.
A voltage applied to the mirror and landing electrodes together. It multiplies the effect of the much smaller address voltage, which the patent calls torque gain.
One, three or two stable mirror positions. The bistable mode, with the mirror resting on one landing electrode or the other, is the digital mode that DLP uses.
Arranging the electrodes so that little torque is left when the mirror tip lands, which reduces impact damage and sticking.
Surfaces in contact sticking together; the reason the patent describes the reset pulses of FIGS. 29-30.
Openings in the mirror metal through which the plasma removes the organic spacer underneath, freeing the mirror.
A sacrificial layer, here photoresist or PMMA, that sets the gap under the mirror and is etched away at the end.
Poly(methyl methacrylate), a polymer used as a resist and protective coating.
Patterning metal by depositing it over a resist pattern and then dissolving the resist, which carries away the metal on top of it.
Depositing a thin metal film by knocking atoms off a target with ions.
As printed; evidently PECVD, plasma-enhanced chemical vapour deposition of oxide.
Aluminum alloyed with small amounts of titanium and silicon, used for both hinge and mirror layers.
Metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor. Here each acts as a switch that connects a column (bitline) to a pixel's address electrode.
Row and column wires of a memory-style array. Selecting a wordline turns on a row of transistors; the bitlines carry the data into them.
Laser-printer style printing: light discharges a charged photoconductive drum in the image pattern, and toner sticks to that pattern.
